narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score of 22.5 was the strongest influence; it sits far below the average of 37.2 among accepted students and strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year and third-year class rankings came next. Placing in the bottom decile for both Year 1 and Year 3 grades, compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students, gave the model another clear signal that you were likely to struggle with the bar exam.

Your high family income worked in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction slightly toward success. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the combined impact of your test score and academic standing.

The decision was based solely on these academic and economic indicators; neither your gender nor race played any role. To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your LSAT score significantly and strengthening your academic performance before reapplying. Consider targeted test preparation, additional coursework, or a post-baccalaureate program to demonstrate that you can perform at the level expected of successful law students.
